Learning-objective map

LO 1. Explain gastrulation: conversion of the bilaminar disc into the trilaminar disc.
LO 2. Explain neurulation, identify the anterior and posterior neuropores, and connect failed closure to neural tube defects.
LO 3. Explain the origin of neural crest cells and list major neural crest derivatives.
LO 4. Describe the major fates of ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm, including paraxial, intermediate, and lateral plate mesoderm.
LO 5. Explain craniocaudal and lateral folding and how folding contributes to body cavities, the gut tube, and heart positioning.

The one sequence to know

Master sequence: bilaminar disc → primitive streak appears → epiblast cells ingress → definitive endoderm forms first → mesoderm forms next → remaining epiblast becomes ectoderm → notochord induces neural plate → neural folds fuse into neural tube and release neural crest → mesoderm regionalizes → the flat disc folds into a cylindrical embryo with a gut tube and body cavities.
Organizing principle
Week 10 Lecture 2 is easiest if you keep asking two questions: (1) which layer is this structure coming from? and (2) where in the embryo is the tissue moving?

1. Gastrulation: turning two layers into three

Starting point

The embryo begins as a bilaminar disc made of epiblast and hypoblast.

Key event

The primitive streak appears in the epiblast and establishes the cranial-caudal axis.

Cell movement

Epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak and primitive groove.

Outcome

The embryo becomes a trilaminar disc made of ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

Cropped lecture diagram: gastrulation converts the bilaminar embryonic disc into a trilaminar disc.
Order of ingressionWhat happensResulting layer
First epiblast cellsReplace hypoblast cellsDefinitive endoderm
Next epiblast cellsSpread between ectoderm and endodermIntraembryonic mesoderm
Epiblast cells left behindRemain on dorsal surfaceEctoderm
Why this matters
Gastrulation is the moment when broad developmental potential starts being converted into body plan. Once the germ layers are established, later organs can be understood mainly as derivatives of those layers.
Exam trap
Hypoblast is not the source of the three germ layers. The lecture emphasizes that epiblast gives rise to ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

2. Neurulation: from ectoderm to neural tube

Core mechanism: the notochord induces overlying dorsal ectoderm to become neural plate → lateral edges elevate into neural folds with a central neural groove → folds fuse to form the neural tube → the neural tube detaches from surface ectoderm.
Cropped lecture diagram: sequence from neural plate to neural groove and fused neural tube.

Inducer

The notochord is a major midline signaling center that helps specify neural ectoderm.

Product

The neural tube is the precursor of the central nervous system.

Neuropores

The temporary openings at the ends of the neural tube are the anterior (rostral) and posterior (caudal) neuropores.

Timing

The lecture places neuropore closure around the end of week 4; the anterior neuropore closes first (about day 25), then the posterior (about day 27).

If closure fails…General consequenceClassic example
Anterior neuroporeSevere cranial neural tube defectAnencephaly
Posterior neuroporeCaudal neural tube defectSpina bifida spectrum
High yield
Neurulation is not just "making a tube." You need to know the sequence (plate → folds/groove → tube), the temporary neuropores, and the clinical significance of failed closure.

3. Neural crest: a migratory population with many derivatives

Cropped lecture diagram: neural crest cells arise at the dorsal-most portion of the neural tube and migrate away after neural fold fusion.
Origin
Cells at the lateral borders of the neural plate are incorporated into the dorsal neural tube. As the neural tube closes, the dorsal-most region gives rise to neural crest cells, which then migrate widely.
Major neural crest derivative categoryExamples emphasized in lecture
Peripheral/autonomic nervous systemSympathetic ganglia, parasympathetic ganglia, enteric neurons, glia
Pigment cellsMelanocytes
Craniofacial/arch derivativesPharyngeal arch-derived bones and connective tissue
Endocrine-related derivativesChromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla
Cardiac/outflow tract contributionsNeural crest contribution to outflow tract region
Clinical connections from lecture examples
Failed enteric neural crest migration → Hirschsprung disease; defective pharyngeal arch / outflow tract neural crest → 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) associations; melanocyte-related crest defects → Waardenburg syndrome.

4. Germ-layer derivatives: the big map

LayerGeneral fateHigh-yield examples
EctodermSurface ectoderm + neural ectodermEpidermis and appendages; CNS via neural tube; PNS-related derivatives via neural crest
MesodermSupportive, muscular, vascular, connective, urogenital, serosal tissuesSomites, kidney/urogenital structures, body wall, heart, blood vessels
EndodermInternal epithelial linings and glandular parenchymaGut tube lining, respiratory epithelium, liver/pancreatic parenchyma, much of bladder/urethral lining

Mesoderm subdivisions

Axial mesoderm

Forms the notochord. The notochord largely regresses but persists as the nucleus pulposus of intervertebral discs.

Paraxial mesoderm

Organizes into somites. In the trunk, somites split into sclerotome (vertebrae/ribs), myotome (skeletal muscle), and dermatome (dermis components).

Intermediate mesoderm

Gives rise mainly to urogenital structures.

Lateral plate mesoderm

Splits into somatic (parietal) and visceral (splanchnic) mesoderm, contributing to body wall, serous membranes, gut wall, and much of cardiovascular support tissue.

Quick memory aid
Mesoderm is the "middle support layer": muscle, connective tissue, bone, blood vessels, serosal linings, and urogenital tissues all point you toward mesoderm.

5. Folding: how the flat disc becomes a body

Core idea: during week 4, the flat embryonic disc is folded in both the craniocaudal and lateral directions, producing a more cylindrical embryo. This rearrangement helps create the gut tube, body cavities, ventral body wall, and the final positions of important organs such as the heart.

Lateral folding

Cropped lecture diagram: lateral folding helps form the ventral body wall and pinches the yolk sac into the forming gut tube.

Somatic mesoderm + ectoderm

Contribute to the ventral body wall.

Visceral mesoderm + endoderm

Wrap around the forming gut tube.

Yolk sac

Gets "pinched" during folding, contributing to incorporation of endoderm into the embryo as the gut tube.

Body cavities

The space maintained between somatic and visceral mesoderm contributes to the intraembryonic coelom and future body cavities.

Head fold

Cropped lecture diagram: head folding moves the developing heart and septum transversum toward the future thoracic region.

The head fold contributes to formation of the foregut and repositions the heart and future diaphragm (septum transversum) toward the thoracic region. It also reshapes the pericardial region of the intraembryonic coelom.

Tail fold

Cropped lecture diagram: tail folding moves the cloacal membrane, allantois, and connecting stalk to the ventral side.

Tail folding contributes to formation of the hindgut and repositions the cloacal membrane, allantois, and connecting stalk. The lecture specifically highlights bladder exstrophy as a defect associated with failure of proper caudal fold closure.

Folding typeMain structural effectClinical / structural consequence of failure
Craniocaudal (head/tail)Forms foregut/hindgut and repositions heart, septum transversum, cloacal structuresAbnormal relationships of cranial/caudal structures; caudal closure defects such as bladder exstrophy
LateralForms ventral body wall; incorporates yolk sac into gut tube; shapes body cavitiesVentral body-wall defects such as omphalocele and gastroschisis

Last 30 seconds: primitive streak = gastrulation; epiblast makes all 3 germ layers; notochord induces neural plate; neural folds fuse into neural tube; dorsal tube gives neural crest; mesoderm subdivides into axial, paraxial, intermediate, lateral plate; folding forms foregut/hindgut, ventral body wall, gut tube, and body cavities.
